name: Souq Waqif
label: Souq Waqif
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Jassim Bin Mohammed Street' (3 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'Mohammed Bin Jassim House' (pois); moved 5 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/3424940793: the OpenStreetMap point 'Souq Waqif'.
notes: Restored traditional market with lanes, cafes and a falcon souq.

text.description: Souq Waqif is a traditional marketplace in central Doha, and one of the easiest places in the city to fill a phone gallery. Its low, earth-coloured buildings, timber beams, lanterns and busy lanes sell spices, garments, handicrafts and souvenirs, with plenty of cafés and restaurants in between. The name means 'the standing market', because traders once set up at the gates to show off their wares. The original buildings date from the late 19th or early 20th century. After a fire in 2003 the souq was rebuilt, with the work finished in 2008 and the aim of keeping its old look. The best-known single frame is from the road in front of the souq. A passing car adds a little movement. Inside, the lantern-lit alleys give neat symmetrical views, and the lights glow blue and yellow after dark. The golden thumb sculpture in the middle of the souq also makes a good subject, with the crowd behind it. Ask before photographing people, and leave out government buildings, security staff and anyone praying.
text.geographic_location: Souq Waqif is in the Al Souq district in the centre of Doha, a short way inland from the Corniche and Souq Waqif Park.
text.directions_text: There are no Underground, tram or similar stops listed for this spot, so go by taxi or on foot to the Al Souq district in central Doha and ask for Souq Waqif or Jassim Bin Mohammed Street. From there the middle of the souq is about 340 m, roughly a 4-5 minute walk east. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the street view. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) inside the lantern-lit alleys and to 2x-3x if your phone has telephoto, to bring the tower closer to the souq frontage.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Jassim Bin Mohammed Street (across the road from the souq, looking east toward the Fanar). The souq frontage in the foreground with the spiral tower of the Abdullah Bin Zaid Al Mahmoud Islamic Cultural Center in the background, ideally with a passing car for motion. For a balanced picture, line yourself up with the mosque.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and put the tower on the central vertical line so the souq frontage sits evenly on either side. Wait for a car to pass through the frame for a touch of motion. For a second picture, go into the souq and shoot straight down a lantern-lit alley so the walls run symmetrically to the centre.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the souq frontage to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky does not wash out. After dark in the alleys, use night mode and hold the phone steady against a wall or post. Live Photos can catch the passing car.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning, midday and late afternoon give similar light on the street view. Early morning is quieter inside the souq, while the alleys look their best in the evening when the lanterns and coloured lights come on.

text.access_note: The street viewpoint is a public road, but shops and venues inside the souq may have their own rules, so check the official site before you go.

name: National Museum of Qatar
label: National Museum Qatar
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Box Park' (1 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Box Park' (way/1145093557): middle (238 m across); moved 5 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q3084218: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.

text.description:
The National Museum of Qatar is the big, sculptural building at the south end of Doha's Corniche. French architect Jean Nouvel took the desert rose crystal as his inspiration, and the result is a cluster of 539 interlocking discs rising from the water's edge. At its heart sits the restored early-20th-century palace of Sheikh Abdullah bin Jassim Al Thani. The current building opened on 28 March 2019, on the site of the earlier museum from 1975.

It sits within a wider raised panorama that also takes in Ras Abu Aboud Stadium and MIA Park. That makes it a good spot for a photo that shows the museum in its setting, and for finding a quieter angle than the ground-level views.

The discs are sand-coloured, so the building looks best when the light is soft and low. If you want the close-up shots, the museum grounds are the alternative: the discs glowing warmly near sunset, or the Qatari flag on its pole set against the architecture. Take a few frames from here first, then decide whether to walk over.
text.geographic_location: The museum stands at the south end of Doha's Corniche, rising from the sea and linked to the shore by bridges.
text.directions_text: No Underground or tram stop is listed for this spot, so check a map app for the best way to reach Box Park. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the full panorama with the stadium and MIA Park. Then try the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to bring the museum's discs closer. The ultra-wide (0.5x) will make the museum very small, so use it only if you want lots of surrounding skyline.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at Box Park (upper floors). A raised panoramic view that takes in the National Museum of Qatar along with the Ras Abu Aboud Stadium and MIA Park. Stand at the side of the floor that faces south and keep clear of anything in the way.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the museum on one of the thirds, leaving the stadium or park to balance the other side. Hold the phone level so the horizon stays straight. For a different view, panorama mode works well for the full sweep. If you later visit the museum itself, look for the discs glowing at sunset, or the Qatari flag against the building.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the museum on screen to focus, then slide the exposure down slightly so the sand-coloured discs keep their detail and the sky doesn't wash out. Hold still when using the telephoto, and rest your elbows on a ledge if there is one.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon towards sunset, when the discs can pick up a warm glow. Avoid the harsh midday light, which flattens the building's shapes.

text.access_note: The museum has its own opening days and photography rules (including limits on flash, tripods and selfie sticks), so check the official site before you go, and check the Box Park viewpoint is open as well.

name: Museum of Islamic Art
label: Museum of Islamic Art
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Al Corniche' (3 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'Al Corniche North Parking' (pois).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/10671567: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Museum of Islamic Art' (236 m across).
notes: I. M. Pei's landmark museum on its own island by the Corniche.

text.description:
The Museum of Islamic Art sits on its own island at one end of Doha's seven-kilometre Corniche, close to the old dhow harbour. Architect I. M. Pei asked for a stand-alone island so that nothing could be built right up against it later. The museum stands on an artificial peninsula about 60 metres off the Corniche, and a crescent-shaped park wraps around it. Pei chose creamy limestone for the outer walls so the stone shows different shades through the day.

The classic view is from the waterfront on Al Corniche, looking across the water. Depending on where you stand, palms may appear in the foreground and the West Bay towers may appear in the background. The museum opened to the public on 8 December 2008 and reopened after a major renovation in October 2022.

On a phone, keep the museum in the middle of the frame and let the water fill the foreground. A little zoom helps to tighten the framing on the museum. If you have time, there are two other good frames. The museum's facade shows a close, symmetrical view with the fountain reflected on the wet paving. MIA Park shows the museum framed by palms and lawns, with the towers behind.
text.geographic_location: On the Corniche waterfront in Doha, at the Dhow Harbour end, looking across the water to the Museum of Islamic Art on its island beside MIA Park, about 2.5 km to the east.
text.directions_text: No Underground or tram stop is listed for this spot, so use a taxi or walk to the Dhow Harbour end of the Corniche. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to take in the water, the shoreline and the distant museum together. Then use a little zoom to tighten the framing on the museum. Use ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you move closer, for the facade and fountain frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Al Corniche (stand east of the Dhow Harbour skyline viewpoint at the northern tip of the harbour, facing the museum across the water). The museum on its island across the water, framed by palms, with the West Bay towers in the background. Palms and the West Bay towers may appear in the view, depending on where you stand.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and place the museum on one of the vertical lines, with the water filling the lower third. If palms are nearby, let a few fronds frame one edge of the picture. For a different view, the museum facade shows the fountain reflected on the wet paving in a close, symmetrical frame, and MIA Park shows the museum with palms and lawns in front.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the museum to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the pale limestone does not turn white. After dark, use night mode and hold the phone steady against a railing or your body.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Blue hour into the night, or sunset. Whether sunrise or sunset gives the better light is best checked on the day.

text.access_note: The Corniche waterfront is a public space with no ticket needed, but for the museum galleries and any photography rules inside, check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: The Corniche viewpoint is public waterfront and needs no ticket.
Palms and the West Bay towers may appear in the view from the Corniche, depending on where you stand.
Blue hour, night and sunset are good times for this view, although sunrise versus sunset is best checked on the day.
Night mode works best with the phone held steady.
Photography rules inside the galleries may be restricted and are shown on signs on site.
A taxi or walking are ways to reach the Dhow Harbour end of the Corniche.

name: The Pearl-Qatar
label: The Pearl-Qatar
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Porto Arabia' (3 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'Sabah w Masa - Porto Arabia branch' (pois); moved 5 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/10926396: large area 'The Pearl-Qatar' (6235 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: Artificial island with marinas and Mediterranean-style architecture.

text.description:
The Pearl-Qatar is an artificial island off Doha, with an area of nearly 4 square kilometres and about 32 kilometres of coastline that did not exist before it was built. It is split into 12 districts, each with its own architectural style, so the look changes noticeably from one corner to the next. The classic photo here is the yacht-filled marina at Porto Arabia, ringed by residential towers. Porto Arabia alone has 31 towers.

From there you look out towards the marina mouth with boats in the foreground and towers on both sides. The Pearl-Qatar itself lies about 734 m to the south-east. The marina photographs best around blue hour, when the water goes glassy and the tower lights reflect in it.

If you have time for a second stop, Qanat Quartier is a quieter alternative. It has canals, pastel Venetian-style facades and 15 bridges, including a replica of the Rialto Bridge. Choose a specific bridge on the map before you shoot. Allow a little extra time to wander, as the island is spread out and the districts are quite different from each other.
text.geographic_location: The Pearl-Qatar is an artificial island off the coast of Doha, and Porto Arabia is one of its main waterfront districts, built around a large marina.
text.directions_text: Head for Porto Arabia on The Pearl Island. The Pearl-Qatar is about 734 m (roughly 10 minutes on foot) to the south-east. Golf carts and boat taxis also run in Porto Arabia if you would rather not walk. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the marina, boats and towers together. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more of the curve of the promenade and the sky. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out a single yacht or a cluster of tower lights.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Porto Arabia (inner arc of the promenade, looking out toward the marina mouth). The Pearl's yacht-filled marina with the surrounding residential towers, best framed at blue hour when the water reflects the lights.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the waterline on the lower third, so the sky and tower lights get the rest of the frame. Keep some boats in the foreground for depth. The two sides of the marina make a natural frame if you stay centred on the marina mouth. For a calmer, more colourful alternative, try the canals and arched bridges of Qanat Quartier.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the brightest part of the water or sky to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the tower lights do not burn out. As it gets dark, use night mode and rest your elbows or phone on the railing to keep it steady. Hold still until the capture finishes.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Blue hour, roughly 30 to 45 minutes after sunset, when the water becomes a mirror and the tower lights balance the sky.

text.access_note: There is no charge for the viewpoint, but check the official site before you go in case of any restrictions or events.

name: Katara Cultural Village
label: Katara
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Katara Mosque' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Katara Mosque' (way/769412277): middle (47 m across); moved 15 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from the Wikipedia article 'Katara Cultural Village'.
notes: Cultural village with an amphitheatre, mosques and a pigeon tower.

text.description: Katara Cultural Village is a cultural and shopping complex on Doha's eastern coast, between West Bay and the Pearl. It opened in 2010 and is built to look like a traditional Qatari village, with low sand-coloured buildings, shaded alleys and courtyards. Guides call Katara Mosque one of the most photographed landmarks in the village. Its turquoise-tiled dome and minaret (guides also describe blue and gold tiles) stand out well against the plain buildings around them. The mosque was designed by the Turkish architect Zainab Fadil Oglu. From the plaza you can photograph the exterior and courtyard, and the dome and minaret fit into one upright frame. Late in the afternoon the sun falls straight onto the tiles, so the blues look at their richest. Elsewhere in the village you can also find a 5,000-seat marble amphitheatre and brick-and-clay pigeon towers about 15 metres high, so it is worth leaving time to wander. Keep your phone ready for people crossing the plaza, and take a few frames with and without them. Inside the mosque is a different matter: photos are not allowed there, and visitors outside prayer times must follow dress rules, so keep your camera for the outside.
text.geographic_location: Katara sits on Doha's eastern coast, between the West Bay district and the Pearl, on the waterfront. The mosque is in the village itself, on the main plaza side.
text.directions_text: There are no Underground or tram stops listed for this spot. Head for Katara Cultural Village, then make your way to the main plaza and the mosque's tiled dome and minaret. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the dome and minaret together. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you are close and the minaret will not fit. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for close-ups of the tilework.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (exterior and courtyard, from the main plaza side). The blue and gold tiled dome and minaret of the mosque, with the tilework lit directly in the late light.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the minaret up with a vertical line so it does not lean. Leave some sky above it. Then move in with the telephoto for a frame filled with mosaic. If you also have time, Katara Amphitheatre makes a second picture: its curved seating and empty stage, with the Gulf beyond.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the tiles to set focus and exposure, then slide the exposure down a little so the tile colours stay rich and the sky is not washed out.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon, when the sun hits the tiles head-on.

text.access_note: The village is a public complex and the mosque's exterior and courtyard are generally fine to photograph, but the inside is restricted and photos are not allowed there; event days may limit photography, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: A phone's ultra-wide lens (0.5x) helps fit a tall minaret into the frame when you stand close.
Lowering the exposure slider helps keep colour in bright tiles against the sky.
The plaza may have other visitors passing through the frame.

name: Khalifa International Stadium
label: Khalifa Stadium
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Aspire Park' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Aspire Park' (way/151612937): edge nearest the subject (1933 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/8677986: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Khalifa International Stadium' (388 m across).
notes: World Cup stadium with a distinctive arch.

text.description:
Khalifa International Stadium is the main home ground of the Qatar men's national football team and a major venue in the Aspire Zone, the sports district in Al Rayyan. It first opened in 1976 and was rebuilt for the 2022 FIFA World Cup, reopening in 2017 with 45,857 seats and a roof over the whole bowl. Its signature feature is a pair of tall arches, one on the east side and one on the west, each over 120 metres high. They give the stadium a clear outline that is easy to recognise even from a distance. It hosted eight matches in the 2022 World Cup, including the third-place play-off.

The stadium is about 388 metres across, so it is hard to fit in from close by. This is why the walkway below the Aspire Tower in Aspire Park works well. From here you get a calm, green foreground of lawn and trees. The tower and the stadium sit together in the wider scene, which tells the story of the whole district rather than just one building. Keep the arches and the tower upright in the frame and leave a little sky above them.

If you want a different angle, The Torch Doha (Aspire Tower) looks down onto the roof and arches through glass. Access to its upper floors is not guaranteed, so check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: The stadium is in Al Rayyan, on the western side of Doha, about 9 km from the centre. It is part of the Aspire Zone sports district, next to the Aspire Tower and the park below it.
text.directions_text: There are no Metro or tram stops listed for this spot, so head for Aspire Park in the Aspire Zone, Al Rayyan. Follow the park paths towards the arches, which are easy to see. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the lawn, the tower and the stadium together. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a cleaner, less stretched view. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the arches and the roof line.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Aspire Park (walkway below the Aspire Tower). A quieter, greener foreground of the Aspire Zone with the tower and stadium visible in the wider district scene. From here the stadium lies to the east, and the tower is part of the same Aspire Zone scene, with green parkland in front.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and use them to keep the tower and arches upright. Put some grass or a path in the bottom third as a foreground, and let the stadium sit further back. For a tighter shot, zoom in on the arch and roof. If you also visit The Torch Doha, you can shoot straight down onto the roof as an alternative, but hold the phone flat against the glass to cut reflections.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the stadium to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky stays blue and the roof keeps its detail. Take a few frames and check them, as the tower and arches can look different with each zoom.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon usually gives softer light and cooler air for walking around the park. Midday sun is harsh, and the sky can look washed out.

text.access_note: Aspire Park is an open public space, but access to the stadium and to The Torch Doha can vary, so check the official site before you go.

name: Msheireb Downtown Doha
label: Msheireb Downtown
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/309833: large area 'Mushayrib Downtown Doha' (1077 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: Modern district built in traditional Qatari style.

text.description:
Msheireb Downtown Doha is a newly built district in the middle of the city, created to renew the old Mushayrib neighbourhood. The name means 'a place to drink water' in Arabic. It covers about 31 hectares and was developed by Msheireb Properties, part of Qatar Foundation, with construction starting in January 2010. Its architects set out to blend lessons from traditional Qatari building with modern technology, so the streets mix new buildings with a more traditional Qatari architectural character.

It photographs well because of the contrast. Clean modern façades sit close to the Heritage Quarter, where traditional courtyard houses have been restored and turned into the Msheireb Museums, which opened to the public in October 2015. The restored Msheireb Eid Prayer Ground, opposite Al Koot Fort, is also part of the area. The mix of old and new buildings gives you strong lines and depth.

The district is large, so treat it as a short walk with several photo stops rather than one single view. Begin from the phone icon on the map and look north into the district, then wander further into the district. Keep your phone's gridlines switched on to keep the tall buildings upright, and look for frames made by archways and street corners. Wipe the lens before you start, as city dust and heat haze can soften pictures.
text.geographic_location: Msheireb Downtown Doha is in central Doha, within the districts of Fereej Mohammed Bin Jasim and Mushayrib. It sits right beside the Amiri Diwan, Souk Waqif and Al Koot Fort.
text.directions_text: No Underground or tram stop is listed for this spot, so start from Souk Waqif or the Amiri Diwan area, both right next to the district, and go by taxi if you are coming from further away. Ask to be dropped at Msheireb Downtown Doha. The phone icon on the map is about 360 m south of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in tall buildings and the width of a street, then switch to the default lens (1x) for most shots. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out façade details, arches and rooflines.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 360 m south of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north. From here you can photograph the district opening up in front of you, then walk towards it for closer shots.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and line up vertical edges with them so the buildings don't lean. Use a street, archway or shaded passage as a natural frame, with a person walking through for scale. In the Heritage Quarter, move closer with the default lens (1x) or telephoto for doorways, courtyards and textures.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on a bright façade to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the sky and white walls keep their detail. Try portrait mode for a person against the buildings, and use night mode after dark, holding the phone steady against a wall or railing.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and cooler walking. After sunset, the lit streets work well with night mode.

text.access_note: The district is made up of streets and public spaces, but museums and individual buildings may have their own rules, so check the official site before you go.

name: Qatar National Library
label: Qatar National Library
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Qatar National Library' (2 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/134742390: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Qatar National Library' (53 m across).
notes: Rem Koolhaas-designed library in Education City.

text.description: Qatar National Library is Doha's national library, a research library and a public library under one roof. It was designed by the Dutch architect Rem Koolhaas of OMA and opened in April 2018 in Education City, the district Qatar Foundation developed for higher education. Photographers like it for its interior. Long rows of bookshelves run away from you into the building, so the shelves act as leading lines and the frame feels calm and symmetrical. By 2026 the library held more than a million books, and it also looks after the Heritage Library, with about 2,400 manuscripts. Outside, the angled, pointed glass facade suits a wide frame, and a high look-down onto the book rooms shows the layered floors. For the classic shot, go inside to the main floor and stand in the top-left corner as you face the entrance, then shoot along the shelves. Keep the phone level and use gridlines so the shelves stay straight. Photographing inside needs permission, so contact the library in advance through qnl.qa and arrange it, and check the official site before you go. To find the spot, use the library's name and the inside-the-building directions. Outside the sun can be strong, so sunglasses are useful between shots.
text.geographic_location: The library stands in Education City, a university and research district of Doha developed by Qatar Foundation.
text.directions_text: No Metro or tram stop is given for this spot; head for Education City in Doha and ask for Qatar National Library by name. Once you arrive, go inside to the main floor and stand in the top-left corner as you face the entrance. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for the bookshelf view, or 2x if your phone has it, which gives the medium-lens look the guides recommend. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) outside to fit the whole angled glass facade into one frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Go inside Qatar National Library, to the main floor, and stand in the top-left corner when facing the entrance. From this corner the photo shows rows of bookshelves receding into the interior, with the shelves as leading lines and a strong sense of symmetry.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Line yourself up with the centre aisle and turn on gridlines so the shelves run straight into the distance. Keep the phone level, since tilting bends the symmetry. For a different view, shoot the angled glass facade from outside in the ultra-wide (0.5x), centred so both sides match. Or take a high look-down onto the rows of books in a book room to show the layered floors. Both interior views need permission.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the middle of the shelves to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the bright areas wash out. Hold the phone steady with both hands, and use night mode only if the interior looks dim.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon gives the most dynamic light, though morning and midday look similar. Outside, the sun is strong, so bring sunglasses.

text.access_note: Photographing inside needs permission arranged in advance with the library, so check the official site (qnl.qa) before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Gridlines and holding the phone level help keep the shelves straight and the view symmetrical.
Dropping the exposure slider slightly can stop bright areas washing out in an interior shot.
Night mode may help if the interior looks dim.

name: Aspire Tower
label: Aspire Tower
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Aspire Park' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Aspire Park' (way/151612937): edge nearest the subject (1933 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/770633250: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Aspire Tower' (99 m across).
notes: Torch-shaped hotel tower in Aspire Zone.

text.description:
Aspire Tower, also called The Torch Doha, is a 300-metre skyscraper hotel in the Aspire Zone complex. It was the focal point of the 15th Asian Games in December 2006 and was completed in November 2007. Its tall, glass-skinned shape makes it a landmark of Aspire Zone. It is currently the second tallest building in Qatar. Higher up, a swimming pool sits 80 metres above the ground and sticks out 12 metres from the façade. The front also carries LED lighting that can change colour.

The best-known phone view is from the lake in Aspire Park, looking back at the tower. From the lake shore you get the tower rising above the water, with its reflection and the park's greenery around it. That makes a tidy, symmetrical picture that works even for a first-time phone photographer. The park's lawns and paths keep the tower in a green setting, and it looks its best in golden hour and after dark, when it is lit up.

Try one wide shot to show the whole scene, then a closer one that focuses on the tower and its reflection. If you want a second angle, a dusk view from the parking area at Villaggio Mall gives a tighter composition with the tower lit. Keep the horizon straight, since the tower is so tall and straight that any tilt shows. Take a few frames, because other visitors or joggers may walk through your shot.
text.geographic_location: Aspire Tower stands in the Aspire Zone complex in Doha, Qatar, close to Khalifa International Stadium. The lake viewpoint is in Aspire Park, to the west of the tower.
text.directions_text: No public transport stop is listed for this spot, so head for Aspire Park in the Aspire Zone area of Doha. From there the tower is to the east, about 460 m away, which is roughly a 5–7 minute walk if you want to walk across to it. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the tower, lake and reflection together. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you are close to the water and the top of the tower will not fit. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for a tighter shot of the tower and its reflection.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Aspire Park (lake shore, looking back toward the tower). The tower rising above the park's lake, with its reflection and the greenery framing it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the tower on one of the vertical lines, with the horizon on a horizontal line so the tower stands straight. Keep a strip of water in the lower part of the frame so the reflection shows. For something different, try a low phone height just above the water. A dusk view from the parking area at Villaggio Mall gives a tighter composition as an alternative.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the tower to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky and the lit façade do not wash out. After dark, use night mode and rest your phone on a wall or rail so it stays steady.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Golden hour, shortly after sunrise or before sunset, when the light is soft. The tower is also lit at night, so a visit after dark works well too.

text.access_note: Aspire Park is a public park and the tower itself is a hotel, so check the official site before you go for any opening times or access to the tower's upper floors.

name: Tornado Tower
label: Tornado Tower
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Al Corniche Street' (2 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'Al Corniche North Parking' (pois).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/152653058: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Tornado Tower' (79 m across).

text.description:
Tornado Tower is a 52-floor office tower in Doha's West Bay business district. It is 195 m tall and was completed in 2008. Its waist narrows in the middle like an hourglass, and its steel-grid skin gives it a twisting look. It is often compared to London's Gherkin. That shape is what makes it easy to pick out in a photo, even among the neighbouring towers.

The classic picture is taken from the Corniche promenade, looking across West Bay. From there the tower rises among the WTC and Burj Qatar towers, with palm trees along the shoreline in the foreground. It is a recognisable skyline view, and morning shots from the Corniche are common.

Walk along the promenade until a palm trunk or lamp post is not cutting across the tower. If you want a different view, the street crossing at Majlis Al Taawon Street and Al Funduq Street shows the tower above the business district and traffic. The foot of the tower is inside a private office complex, so keep a respectful distance from entrances and restricted areas.
text.geographic_location: Tornado Tower stands in the West Bay business district of Doha, among the other high-rise towers of West Bay. The Corniche promenade runs along the shoreline south-west of it.
text.directions_text: No Metro or tram stops are listed nearby, so go by taxi to Al Corniche Street, on the Corniche promenade. From there the tower is to the north-east, about 2.1 km away on foot if you want to walk on towards West Bay. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the tower itself. At the default lens (1x) it will look small and far away across the water.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Al Corniche Street (Corniche promenade, looking across West Bay). The tower rises among the WTC and Burj Qatar towers above palm trees along the shoreline, a classic West Bay skyline view. The tower is to the north-east.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and put the tower on one of the vertical lines, with the palms along the bottom edge. Keep the phone level so the tall towers do not lean. For a wider skyline, step back to the default lens (1x) and include the neighbouring towers. As an alternative, try the crossing of Majlis Al Taawon Street and Al Funduq Street for a city view.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the tower to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky does not turn white and the steel grid stays visible. Hold the phone steady with both hands when zoomed in.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning is a popular time for this view. Evening and night shots are also worth trying, with night mode on and the phone braced against a railing.

text.access_note: The Corniche promenade is a public space, but the foot of the tower is inside a private office complex, so check the official site before you go if you want to get closer.

name: Fanar, Qatar Islamic Cultural Center
label: Fanar Mosque
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Souq Waqif Park' (2 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'Parisa Souq Waqif' (pois); moved 15 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OSM R10664399 (Fanar Qatar Islamic Cultural Center): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.

text.description:
The Fanar, Qatar Islamic Cultural Center is best known for its spiral minaret, which stands out above the buildings around it. After dark the minaret is lit, and that is when it makes the strongest photograph. A well-known view is from the Souq Waqif side, where the glowing tower sits above the souq area and gives you a ready-made backdrop.

For a phone photo, the simplest plan is to stand in Souq Waqif Park and look to the north-east. A night panorama from Souq Waqif Park is a good way to capture the lit minaret with the surrounding skyline. Take a few frames at different zoom levels: the default lens (1x) for the whole scene, and the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the spiral on its own.

If you would like a different angle, the Doha Skyline Viewpoint shows the West Bay skyline across the water with the minaret in the old-town part of the frame. Mina Corniche is a quieter stretch of waterfront with a similar view. In both places the Fanar is a smaller part of the picture, so zoom in to give it more weight.

If you want to photograph inside, ask the staff first, as interior photography may be restricted, especially in the prayer areas.
text.geographic_location: The Fanar is in the old-town part of central Doha, close to Souq Waqif.
text.directions_text: Head for Souq Waqif and walk to the park. The minaret is easy to pick out, especially after dark when it is lit. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to take in the minaret and the souq area around it. Switch to the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to fill the frame with the spiral. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want a lot of foreground, as it will make the tower look small.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Souq Waqif Park. A night panorama looking across to the Fanar building, with its lit spiral minaret rising above the surrounding area.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and place the minaret on one of the vertical lines, leaving some sky above it. Try a panorama to include the souq-side buildings and the tower together, moving the phone slowly and evenly. If you want a different angle, the Doha Skyline Viewpoint and Mina Corniche both show the minaret across the water as part of a wider skyline.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: After dark, use night mode and rest your elbows or the phone on a wall or railing to keep it still. Tap the minaret to focus, then lower the exposure slider a little so the lights do not wash out the spiral.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: After dark, when the minaret is lit.

text.access_note: Interior photography may be restricted, so ask staff before shooting inside the prayer areas.

name: Al Koot Fort
label: Al Koot Fort
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Al Koot Fort' (4 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/2155761: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'al Koot Fort' (70 m across).
notes: Small historic fort beside Souq Waqif.

text.description:
Al Koot Fort, also called the Doha Fort, is a whitewashed fort with corner towers and battlements, set among the lanes of Souq Waqif. The version you see today was rebuilt in 1927 by Sheikh Abdulla bin Qassim Al Thani after the Ottomans had left. It was renovated in 1978 and later became a museum of Qatari crafts, fishing gear and old photographs of daily life. It is one of the most useful quick stops on this map because the pale walls and towers read clearly even on a small phone screen.

The best-known view is from the front, where you stand at the front of the fort with a fountain and small park with benches in the foreground. The fountain and benches make a natural foreground, and the straight walls and regular battlements suit the phone's gridlines. The inside is usually closed, so most visitors photograph the outside, which works well for this spot. Come in the evening if you can, when the fort is lit up and the walls glow against the darkening sky. Golden hour or blue hour is a good choice. Plan on a few minutes: take one wide shot of the whole fort, then step closer for the towers and battlements. If the fountain is switched off or there is fencing around the site, simply move along the park edge for a cleaner angle.
text.geographic_location: In the Al Bidda neighbourhood of central Doha, in the middle of Souq Waqif and close to the Corniche.
text.directions_text: No Metro or tram stop is listed for this spot, so go by taxi and ask for Souq Waqif. The fort stands in the middle of the souq, and the phone icon on the map is at the front of the fort, facing the fountain and small park. Once you are in the souq, follow the lanes towards the fort; its pale walls and towers are easy to spot. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole fort with the fountain in front. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you are close and the towers will not fit. Use the telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for the battlements and tower tops.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From here you see the whitewashed walls, corner towers and battlements, with the fountain and benches in front.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the base of the walls up with a horizontal line so the fort does not lean. Keep the fountain and benches low in the frame to give depth. For a closer picture, use the telephoto on one corner tower and the battlements against the sky.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the fort wall to focus, then lower the exposure slider a little so the white walls keep their detail. In the evening, use night mode and hold the phone steady against something solid while it takes the picture.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Evening, when the fort is lit up. Golden hour or blue hour also works well.

text.access_note: The outside can be photographed freely from the park, but the interior is generally closed and there may be building work nearby, so check the official site before you go.

name: Doha Corniche
label: Doha Corniche
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q1234812: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Waterfront promenade with views of the West Bay skyline.

text.description:
The Doha Corniche is a seven-kilometre waterfront promenade that follows the curve of Doha Bay. It runs from the towers of Al Dafna and West Bay in the north to the older districts near Souq Waqif in the south. A road runs alongside the walkway, but the long strip of open space is what makes it work for photos. The bay curves away in front of you, with the skyline set above the water.

The Corniche is also where Qatar holds its big public events, including the National Day Parade, so it carries a lot of civic meaning as well as being a pleasant place for a stroll. Much of the land here was reclaimed from the sea from the late 1960s onwards. The Sheraton hotel, which opened in February 1982 on a specially made island, became an early symbol of the new waterfront. The brutalist Central Post Office from 1988 is another landmark along the route.

For a phone, the main job is to show the sweep of the bay and the sense of space. Use the long curve of the path, railings or kerb as lines that lead the eye along the waterfront. Keep the horizon level using the gridlines. Walk a few steps along the promenade rather than shooting only from one spot, because the angle of the curve changes the view of the towers. Check the screen for reflections and glare off the water before you press the shutter.
text.geographic_location: The Corniche wraps around Doha Bay in the centre of Doha, linking the Al Dafna business district in the north with the old quarters near Souq Waqif in the south.
text.directions_text: From there the Corniche point is 298 m to the east, about 5 minutes on foot. Head east towards the Corniche point on the map. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the curve of the bay and the skyline together. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) to capture the full length of the promenade and its leading lines. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out individual towers or buildings across the water.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Dhow Harbour (northern tip of the harbour, facing east across the water toward the Museum of Islamic Art). The Museum of Islamic Art and the West Bay skyline in one frame, with moored dhows in the foreground. Shoot back along the promenade or out across the water.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and place the horizon on the upper or lower line. Use the edge of the path or the railing as a line leading into the picture. Keep the phone level so the skyline does not tilt. If people are walking by, wait for a gap or include one or two to show the scale.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the skyline to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the sky or water is bright, so the buildings keep their detail. After dark, use night mode and brace your elbows against your body or rest the phone on a solid surface to keep it still.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon is usually more comfortable for walking and gives softer light. The evening, when the city lights come on, suits night mode.

text.access_note: The Corniche is an open public promenade, though events can close sections, so check the official site before you go if you are visiting on a special occasion.
claims_not_in_sources: Early morning and late afternoon usually give softer light and more comfortable walking conditions in Doha.
The city lights come on in the evening, which suits night mode.
Events can sometimes close sections of the Corniche.

name: West Bay
label: West Bay skyline
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q7984405: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Skyscraper district seen across the bay.

text.description:
West Bay is the part of Doha where the city looks most modern. It runs along the east coast and takes in Al Qassar, Al Dafna, West Bay Lagoon and Onaiza, and most of Qatar's tallest skyscrapers stand here. The land itself is fairly new. It was dredged and reclaimed in the late 1970s, north of the older city, and some locals still call it dafna, an Arabic word meaning landfill. One of its first big landmarks, the Sheraton Grand Doha Resort & Convention Hotel, began going up in 1978 and was finished in 1981. It shaped the skyline for years before the towers around it arrived.

The area photographs well because the buildings are tall, close together and very different in shape, so a single frame can show a whole row of glass and steel. Start wide with the ultra-wide lens (0.5x) to get the full skyline, then try the default lens (1x) for a tidier group of towers. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out rooflines and details. Keep the phone level, because tall buildings look like they are leaning if you tilt it upwards, and the gridlines will help you with this.
text.geographic_location: West Bay is on Doha's east coast, north of the older city centre. It covers the districts of Al Qassar, Al Dafna, West Bay Lagoon and Onaiza.
text.directions_text: No Underground or tram stop is listed for this spot, so start from central Doha near the Corniche and take a taxi north to West Bay. Ask to be dropped. From there the middle of West Bay is 461 m to the south, a short walk. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the whole skyline, then switch to the default lens (1x) for a cleaner group of towers. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for rooftops and details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Doha Skyline Viewpoint (along the Corniche promenade, across the harbour from the Museum of Islamic Art). An unobstructed view across the water of the West Bay towers, well suited to skyline and night shots.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line up the edges of the towers with the vertical lines so they stay straight. Hold the phone level rather than tilting it up. Put some open foreground, such as water, paving or sky, at the bottom of the frame so the buildings have room to stand up. Try a second shot with the telephoto lens to isolate two or three towers.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on a tower to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky keeps its colour and the glass does not turn white. Use panorama mode only if you can pan slowly and keep the phone upright.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on the glass. Around dusk, when the buildings are lit, switch on night mode and brace your elbows against your body to keep the phone steady.

text.access_note: West Bay is a normal urban district, but individual buildings, hotels and viewing areas may have their own access rules, so check the official site before you go.

name: Imam Muhammad ibn Abd al-Wahhab Mosque
label: State Mosque
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Imam Muhammad ibn Abd al-Wahhab Mosque' (2 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q12242846: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Qatar's national mosque with many domes.

text.description:
This is the national mosque of Qatar, also called the Qatar State Mosque or the Grand Mosque of Doha. It opened in 2011 and is built in a traditional Arab style with modern touches. It is large: the central hall has 28 big domes, the outer quadrangle has 65 smaller ones, and the arcades are lit at night by hanging copper chandeliers. The grounds are ringed by a belt of trees and have parking for about 3,000 cars.

It photographs well for two reasons. The building is a handsome subject in its own right, with domes, arcades and a minaret. It also stands on raised ground, so from the grounds and the edge of the parking area you can look out across Doha's skyline with the mosque in the foreground. That combination gives you a wide city view with something solid and interesting in front of it.

For a phone, the skyline view is the main prize. For a close-up of the building, walk to the open plaza in front and frame the domes and arcades from there. Keep to the outside: photography inside the mosque is generally not allowed. Be ready to shoot quickly and politely, as security staff are on site and visitor access is limited around prayer times.
text.geographic_location: The mosque is in the Lejbailat district of Doha. It sits on raised ground inside its own grounds, surrounded by a green belt of trees and a very large parking area.
text.directions_text: No Metro or tram stop is listed for this spot, so go by taxi or private car to the Lejbailat district of Doha and ask for the Imam Muhammad ibn Abd al-Wahhab Mosque, also known as the Qatar State Mosque. Once there, head for the raised grounds and the parking area to find the phone icon on the map. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for the skyline with the mosque in the foreground. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) on the plaza to fit the domes, arcades and minaret into one frame. If your phone has a telephoto (2x-5x), use it to pick out the towers of the skyline.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From here the photo shows a panoramic Doha skyline with the mosque building in the foreground. For a second view, walk to the open plaza in front of the building and frame the domes, arcades and minaret.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and place the horizon on the upper or lower line, so the skyline does not cut the picture in half. Let part of the mosque fill one side of the frame to give the city a foreground. On the plaza, step back and use ultra-wide (0.5x), keeping the phone level so the arcades do not lean.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the skyline to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little at sunset so the sky keeps its colour. After dark, use night mode and rest your elbows on a wall or railing to keep still. Panorama mode works well for the full city sweep. Do not rely on a tripod, as security staff may not allow one.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Sunset and after dark, when the city lights come on.

text.access_note: This is a working place of worship: visitor access is limited at prayer times and a conservative dress code applies, so check the official site before you go.

name: 7 (sculpture)
label: 7 sculpture
camera_source: Researched viewpoint '7' (3 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'The 7 Sculpture By Richard Serra' (pois).
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q7328968: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Richard Serra's seven steel plates near the Museum of Islamic Art.

text.description:
Richard Serra's 7 is a tall tower of weathered steel at the end of a man-made pier in the Museum of Islamic Art Park. It is about 24 metres (80 feet) high, which makes it the tallest public artwork in Qatar. It was unveiled in December 2011. Seven steel plates form a seven-sided shape, a nod to the number seven in Islamic culture and to the minarets of the Muslim world. Three triangular openings let you see out to the sea and the city. The pier itself was built for the sculpture, using leftover material from the museum's construction.

It photographs well because you can walk inside. Stand in the middle, look straight up, and the sky is framed by the opening at the top. From the plaza at the base you also get a wide view of the Doha skyline across the water. The steel was designed to darken naturally from orange to a deep shade over about eight years, so the colour you see may differ from older pictures. For a second, more classic view, walk back along the pier to MIA Park. From there the sculpture stands at the end of the pier, with the water and the West Bay towers behind or beside it. Try both: an inside-looking-up shot and an outside-looking-in shot make a good pair.
text.geographic_location: In the Museum of Islamic Art Park on the Doha corniche, at the end of a pier that extends into the water beside the Museum of Islamic Art.
text.directions_text: No Metro or tram stop is listed for this spot. It is reached on foot from the Museum of Islamic Art. From the museum, walk through the park and out along the pier to the plaza at its end, where the sculpture stands. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) lens for the shot from inside, then the default lens (1x) for the sculpture seen from the pier. The telephoto (2x-5x) is useful for picking out the skyline across the water.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (base of the sculpture, on the plaza at the end of the pier). Looking up from inside the seven-sided steel form, with the sky framed by the opening at the top, and the Doha skyline visible through the openings.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and hold the phone pointing straight up so the opening sits in the middle of the frame and the steel walls lead towards it. For an alternative view, walk back to MIA Park and photograph the sculpture at the end of the pier with the water and the West Bay towers behind or beside it.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest part of the sky to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky stays blue and the steel keeps its rust-brown colour. Keep your fingers clear of the lens when pointing upwards.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: No fixed time is needed. Choose a clear spell for a strong blue sky in the opening. Early or late in the day the steel looks warmer, and the sun is lower so there is less harsh glare.

text.access_note: It is a free public artwork reached on foot through the museum park; check the official site before you go in case of closures or works.
